provenance.authorship: Original project scenario, AI-assisted draft. Practitioner review and calibration pending.

title: Marketing Analyst: Review a Campaign Winner Claim
prompt: Fictional Summit Training tested two landing-page messages for a course. Variant A: 1,000 visits, 100 enquiry forms, 20 confirmed bookings, $500 ad spend. Variant B: 1,000 visits, 150 enquiry forms, 15 confirmed bookings, $500 ad spend. The business goal is confirmed bookings at sustainable acquisition cost. An AI summary says, "B wins because enquiries rose 50%; move the entire budget to B." Review the claim, calculate useful measures, and recommend a next decision without inventing profitability or statistical certainty.
blurb: Evaluate a campaign using booking cost, comparable follow-up, and evidence needed for the next spending decision.

rubric.label: Calculate goal-aligned measures
rubric.description: Uses bookings and cost alongside the enquiry funnel.

anchors.0: Selects B solely on enquiry count or calculates bookings per enquiry incorrectly.
anchors.2: Calculates A at 2% booking conversion and $25 per booking, B at 1.5% and about $33.33 based on current observations.
anchors.4: Also identifies 10% versus 15% enquiry conversion and 20% versus 10% enquiry-to-booking conversion, labeling all booking comparisons as provisional because follow-up differs.

rubric.label: Inspect the comparison design
rubric.description: Identifies confounding and incomplete outcome observation.

anchors.0: Calls either variant a proven causal winner from the current totals.
anchors.2: Flags nonrandom timing and B’s shorter follow-up.
anchors.4: Explains weekday/weekend audience differences and immature bookings separately, waits for comparable outcome windows, and avoids treating equal visit counts as equivalent audiences.

rubric.label: Recommend a proportionate next step
rubric.description: Connects uncertainty to an operational test and economic limits.

anchors.0: Moves all spend immediately or declares profitability without margin data.
anchors.2: Recommends completing follow-up and testing concurrently.
anchors.4: Defines the booking metric and observation window before the next test, uses comparable or randomized allocation if feasible, retains bounded spend, and identifies cancellation and margin evidence needed for a sustainable-cost decision.

reference.scenario: Fictional Summit Training tested two landing-page messages for a course. Variant A: 1,000 visits, 100 enquiry forms, 20 confirmed bookings, $500 ad spend. Variant B: 1,000 visits, 150 enquiry forms, 15 confirmed bookings, $500 ad spend. The business goal is confirmed bookings at sustainable acquisition cost. An AI summary says, "B wins because enquiries rose 50%; move the entire budget to B." Review the claim, calculate useful measures, and recommend a next decision without inventing profitability or statistical certainty.

facts.value: A ran during weekdays and B during the weekend; visitors were not randomly assigned. Confirmed bookings are measured after seven days, but B has only three days of follow-up so far.
facts.reveal_when: candidate asks about assignment, timing, or outcome maturity

facts.value: Course capacity and booking revenue are the same for the two variants, but revenue amount, contribution margin, and cancellations are not supplied. The team can run both messages concurrently for a further week.
facts.reveal_when: candidate asks about economics, cancellations, or a better test

model_points: Enquiries rose from 100 to 150, a 50% relative increase, but the stated outcome is confirmed bookings. Current observed cost per booking is $25 for A and $500/15, approximately $33.33, for B.

The current booking measures do not settle a winner: B has four fewer days of maturation, and weekday versus weekend placement confounds the audience and time comparison. Neither higher enquiries nor current booking cost proves a treatment effect.

Wait for equal follow-up and run messages concurrently with comparable assignment, ideally random where feasible. Predefine booking outcomes and guardrails; without margin and cancellations, a cost figure cannot establish sustainable profitability.

probes.trigger: candidate reverses the winner immediately to A
probes.question: What effect could B’s shorter follow-up have on the observed bookings?

probes.trigger: candidate calls $25 a profitable acquisition cost
probes.question: What revenue, margin, and cancellation evidence do you have?

fair_alternatives: Keeping the current budget split while outcomes mature is reasonable if spend remains within the team’s authority.
A bounded pilot with a documented decision threshold is acceptable; no particular statistical test is required without a justified design and assumptions.
red_flags: Selects B solely on enquiry count or calculates bookings per enquiry incorrectly.
Calls either variant a proven causal winner from the current totals.
Moves all spend immediately or declares profitability without margin data.
follow_ups: Write a 100-word memo separating current metrics, comparison limits, and the next budget decision.
reference.exemplar_answer: B has more enquiries, but the goal is bookings. So far A converts 2% of visits at $25 per booking and B converts 1.5% at about $33.33; those are provisional because B has only three days of follow-up. The weekday/weekend split also prevents a clean causal comparison. I would avoid moving the entire budget, finish equal follow-up, and run a concurrent comparable test with a predefined booking window. Margin and cancellation data are still needed to judge sustainable acquisition cost.

interviewer_notes: Let the candidate use approximate arithmetic. The AI summary is intentionally incomplete; do not invent significance levels, margin, or future bookings. Assess metric selection and design reasoning. Use only supplied facts; say when something is unknown. Accept plain language and equivalent approaches. Assess the demonstrated decisions, not accent, confidence, credentials, or access to particular employers. This is a fictional exercise; do not imply real actions were performed.
